# Getting Started {.unnumbered}

## The Console

On our first interaction with R we are going to learn how to use the console. When you see the console the following message will appear when opening it for the first time.

![](pictures/console.png){fig-align="center" width="377"}

This message shows us relevant information:

- R version code number
- Release date of the version
- R version nickname
- System we are working in (platform)

In addition we can see the **prompt**:

```
>
```

When this symbol appears the console is asking as for inputs, here we can write code and commands so they are executed. Let's do an example typing the word `version` and press enter, you will see something similar to this output.

![](pictures/console_version.png){fig-align="center" width="377"}

See that, when the order execution has ended, the console shows the **prompt** again so we can type more orders to be executed.

### R as a calculator

Type this computation `100*23` on the console and press enter...




::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code  code-line-numbers="false"}
100*23
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 2300
```


:::
:::




When executing the operation the console will return the output of the operation.

::: callout-caution
# Examples

Try the following commands on your console... What is the output? What they do?




::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code  code-line-numbers="false"}
1000:1020
```
:::

::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code  code-line-numbers="false"}
(7 + 7) / 7 * 2 - 4
```
:::



:::

## Using Scripts

In RStudio we can work with multiple file types. The most common file will be the R script. An script for R will use the **.R** extension in the file name, for example *myscript.R*

For creating an script you can go to new file icon on the left corner in RStudio and select R Script option.

![](pictures/script_creation.png){width="800" fig-align="center"}

Your new script will appear on the editor tab, you can have multiple scripts open. Inside the script you can write code and comments, all needs to be saved each time so it can be executed later. For saving you can use save command: `CTRL+S` (Windows) or `command+S` (macOS), or simply selecting save icon.

::: {layout-ncol="2"}
![Unsaved script name color is red](pictures/script_unsaved.png){width="400" style="margin-left:100px;"}

![Saved script name is black](pictures/script_saved.png){width="400" style="margin-left:100px;"}
:::

Let's create an script and include the following code...




::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code  code-line-numbers="false"}
# This is a comment
# Sum all numbers from 1 to 100
sum(1:100)
```
:::




In the script we have included comments, they are types starting with `#`. You can differentiate a comment from code by the color being displayed on the editor. Comments are not readed when the code is executed so here we can type anything we want to make the code more clear.

::: callout-tip
Everyone codes differently and comments helps understanding code written from different programmers, and can always help you understand your own code after some time... **Take time to add comments to your code always!**
:::

Try to execute the code of your script, for doing that you can use the run icon located on the top right corner of the file pane:

![](pictures/script_run.png)

When execute it you will see that the code is copied on the console and then executed, the output is also shown there.

![](pictures/script_output.png)

### File Naming and Extensions

Do not use special characters, blank spaces when naming files, folders. This will avoid problems when installing and executing code in the future. 

A file extension is the text you can find below the file name, for example in `synopsis.txt`, the `.txt` part tell us is a text file. Scripts of R use `.R` extension, this way we can see that is an R script with code. 

::: callout-tip
# Display File Extensions

It is strongly recommended to show file extensions on all the files. Generally, this extensions are visible in majority of operative systems, for Windows users it is hidden by default, but you can change it using [**this tutorial**](https://www.howtogeek.com/205086/beginner-how-to-make-windows-show-file-extensions/).
:::
